sections.heading: Drainage and Land Grading for Farm Operations
sections.body:
Bellhouse Excavating provides agricultural drainage and land grading services for farm operations across Brant County and Brantford. When fields hold water after rain, laneways flood, yards stay soft, or ditches have silted in and stopped carrying water, the problem is usually surface drainage that was never properly graded or maintained.

Agricultural drainage work covers surface grading to redirect standing water, farm ditch cleaning and reshaping, drainage swale construction, culvert installation and replacement, land levelling, and low-spot filling. Bellhouse handles the earthwork with equipment sized for farm properties — including the Volvo A35 for wet-ground access when standard trucks can't get into the field. The goal is farmland that drains predictably, stays workable longer after rain, and doesn't lose productive acres to standing water.

cards.title: Surface drainage correction on farm fields
cards.body: A strong fit when fields have low spots, wheel-track depressions, or areas where water sits after rain instead of draining off. Surface grading redirects water to ditches or drainage paths so the field dries faster and stays workable longer during wet seasons.
cards.outcome: Fields drain more predictably and lose fewer working days to standing water after rain events.

cards.title: Farm ditch cleaning and reshaping
cards.body: Useful when ditches along field edges, farm roads, or property lines have silted in, grown over, or lost their profile. Cleaning and reshaping restores the ditch capacity so water moves off the fields and laneways instead of backing up.
cards.outcome: Ditches carry water at their designed capacity instead of overflowing onto fields and laneways.

cards.title: Farm laneway and yard drainage
cards.body: A practical fit when farm laneways, barn yards, or equipment staging areas have chronic drainage problems — soft spots, pooling water, or mud that limits access during wet weather. Grading and drainage improvements keep these areas functional year-round.
cards.outcome: Laneways and yards stay accessible and functional instead of becoming impassable during wet conditions.

cards.title: Municipal drain coordination
cards.body: A strong fit when drainage work involves or connects to a municipal drain. Bellhouse can handle the excavation and grading scope while the landowner coordinates the required municipal drain approvals and notifications.
cards.outcome: The drainage work meets the practical requirements while the landowner maintains compliance with municipal drain obligations.

items.title: Surface Grading to Redirect Standing Water

sections.heading: Best Fit & Not the Best Fit
sections.subheading: Agricultural drainage and land grading works best on farm properties where surface water is the problem and the solution involves grading, ditch work, and culverts.

items.title: Best fit: Cash crop farms with standing water or wet spots reducing yield
items.body: Fields where low spots, poor surface grades, or silted ditches cause water to sit after rain, delaying planting, reducing yield, and shortening the working season. Common across Brant County, Norfolk County, and Oxford County farmland.

items.title: Best fit: Farm laneways and yards with chronic drainage problems
items.body: Laneways, barn yards, and equipment areas that turn to mud or pool water during wet weather. Grading and drainage improvements keep these areas functional and accessible year-round.

items.title: Best fit: Ditch cleaning along farm roads and field edges
items.body: Ditches that have silted in, grown over, or lost their profile and are no longer carrying water effectively. Cleaning and reshaping restores capacity and prevents water from backing up onto fields.

items.title: Best fit: Land grading to improve surface runoff across fields
items.body: Fields with uneven surfaces, wheel-track depressions, or areas where the natural grade doesn't move water toward the ditches. Surface grading corrects the flow path without requiring tile drainage.

items.title: Best fit: Properties near municipal drains requiring ditch maintenance
items.body: Farm properties where drainage work connects to or runs along a municipal drain. Bellhouse handles the excavation while the landowner manages the Drainage Act requirements.

items.title: Not the best fit: Tile drainage installation
items.body: Bellhouse does not install tile drainage systems. Tile drainage requires specialized tile plows and GPS-guided installation equipment. A dedicated tile drainage contractor is the right fit for systematic tile installation.

items.title: Not the best fit: Urban stormwater management systems
items.body: Engineered urban stormwater systems with catch basins, storm sewers, and retention ponds designed by a stormwater engineer are outside Bellhouse's agricultural drainage scope.

items.title: Not the best fit: Wetland work requiring conservation authority approvals without prior permitting
items.body: Drainage work in or near regulated wetlands, watercourses, or conservation authority regulated areas may require permits before any excavation can begin. Bellhouse can review site conditions, but approvals must be in place before the work starts.

factors.title: Area to grade
factors.body: Larger areas with more ground to level, fill, or reshape require more machine time and more material handling.

factors.title: Ditch length and condition
factors.body: Longer ditches and ditches that are heavily silted or overgrown take more time to clean and reshape. Ditch depth and profile affect the volume of material to handle.

factors.title: Culvert needs
factors.body: Each culvert installation or replacement adds excavation, pipe, backfill, and surface restoration. Upsizing an existing culvert costs more than a simple cleanout.

factors.title: Existing drainage infrastructure
factors.body: Properties with existing ditches and drainage paths that just need cleaning are different from properties where new drainage routes need to be cut from scratch.

factors.title: Wet-ground access challenges
factors.body: Fields and ditches that are only accessible with the A35 or tracked equipment due to soft or saturated ground conditions affect the equipment and approach required.

sections.heading: Farm drainage starts with understanding where the water goes — and why it isn't getting there.
sections.body: Agricultural drainage work is not just digging ditches. Bellhouse reviews the field grades, existing ditch profiles, culvert capacity, and water flow paths to identify why water is sitting where it shouldn't be. The fix is planned around the actual drainage pattern — grading, ditch cleaning, swale construction, and culvert work are coordinated so the water has a clear path off the field and the solution holds through wet seasons.

sections.heading: What Proper Agricultural Drainage Prevents
sections.subheading: Poor drainage on farmland costs yield, working days, and money — and the problems compound over time if the drainage is never properly addressed.

items.problem: Fields that hold water in the same low spots every spring, delaying planting and reducing yield on those acres.
items.solution: Bellhouse grades the low spots, reshapes the field surface, and ensures water has a clear path to the ditches so the field drains consistently.

items.problem: Ditches that have silted in and no longer carry water away from the fields, causing backup and flooding during rain events.
items.solution: Ditches are cleaned to their original profile, silt is removed, and the ditch banks are reshaped so water flows at the designed capacity.

items.problem: Farm laneways and yards that become impassable during wet weather because the surface grades direct water toward traffic areas instead of away from them.
items.solution: Laneway and yard grades are corrected so water moves to ditches and swales instead of pooling on the driving surface and around buildings.

items.question: How do you fix standing water on a farm field in Ontario?
items.answer: Standing water on a farm field is usually caused by low spots in the field surface, poor natural grade that doesn't move water toward the ditches, silted-in ditches that have lost capacity, or undersized culverts that back up during rain events. Bellhouse fixes these problems with surface grading to eliminate low spots and direct water toward drainage paths, ditch cleaning and reshaping to restore flow capacity, culvert installation or replacement at ditch crossings, and swale construction to create new drainage routes where needed. The approach depends on the specific drainage problem — a single low spot in a field is different from a systemic grade issue across forty acres.

items.question: What's the difference between surface drainage and tile drainage?
items.answer: Surface drainage is earthwork — grading the land surface, cleaning ditches, building swales, and installing culverts so water flows across the surface and into drainage paths. Tile drainage is underground — perforated pipe installed below the root zone to lower the water table and drain saturated soil from below. Bellhouse handles surface drainage — the grading, ditch cleaning, and culvert work. Tile drainage requires specialized tile plows and GPS-guided installation equipment operated by a dedicated tile drainage contractor. Many farms benefit from both — surface drainage moves the water that sits on top, and tile drainage handles the water trapped in the soil profile.

items.question: How much does farm ditch cleaning cost in Brant County?
items.answer: Farm ditch cleaning cost depends on the ditch length, how heavily silted or overgrown the ditch is, the depth and profile required, whether culverts need to be replaced, and where the spoil material can be placed. A short stretch of lightly silted ditch with good access is a different scope than a half-mile of heavily silted and overgrown ditch that needs full reshaping. Bellhouse quotes after reviewing the ditch conditions, access, and what the finished ditch needs to handle. Photos of the ditch and a description of the drainage problem help Bellhouse return an accurate number.

items.question: What are the rules around municipal drains in Ontario?
items.answer: Municipal drains in Ontario are governed by the Drainage Act. If your property has a municipal drain on it or adjacent to it, there are requirements around maintenance, alteration, and connecting to the drain. The municipality typically manages the drain through an appointed drainage superintendent. If you need to do work on or near a municipal drain — cleaning, widening, installing a culvert, or changing the flow — you should contact your municipality first to confirm what approvals or notifications are needed. Bellhouse can handle the excavation and grading work, but the landowner is responsible for the Drainage Act compliance and municipal notifications.

items.question: Can you grade land to improve drainage without tile?
items.answer: Yes. Surface grading alone can significantly improve field drainage on many farms. If the problem is water sitting in low spots, running the wrong direction, or pooling because the field surface is uneven, grading can fix it without tile. Bellhouse uses a dozer and excavator to regrade the field surface so water moves toward the ditches and drainage paths naturally. This doesn't replace tile drainage for fields with high water tables or saturated subsoil, but for surface water problems — standing puddles, wheel-track depressions, and poor runoff flow — grading is often the most cost-effective solution.
